triples.head: DNA
triples.evidence: The elucidation of the structure of the double helix provided a hint as to how DNA divides and makes copies of itself.

triples.head: DNA
triples.evidence: The double-helix model suggests that the two strands of the double helix separate during replication, and each strand serves as a template from which the new complementary strand is copied.

triples.head: DNA
triples.evidence: The double-helix model suggests that the two strands of the double helix separate during replication, and each strand serves as a template from which the new complementary strand is copied.

triples.head: conservative replication
triples.evidence: In conservative replication, the parental DNA remains together, and the newly formed daughter strands are together.

triples.head: semi-conservative method
triples.evidence: The semi-conservative method suggests that each of the two parental DNA strands acts as a template for new DNA to be synthesized; after replication, each double-stranded DNA includes one parental or “old” strand and one “new” strand.

triples.head: dispersive model
triples.evidence: In the dispersive model, both copies of DNA have double-stranded segments of parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA interspersed.

triples.head: Meselson and Stahl
triples.evidence: Meselson and Stahl were interested in understanding how DNA replicates. They grew E. coli for several generations in a medium containing a “heavy” isotope of nitrogen (15N), which gets incorporated into nitrogenous bases, and eventually into the DNA (Figure 14.13).
